'''Victoria Michelle Kaspi''' (born June 30, 1967) is a Canadian [[Astrophysics|astrophysicist]] and a professor at [[McGill University]]. Her research primarily concerns [[neutron star]]s and [[pulsar]]s.<ref name="pmv">[http://www.prixduquebec.gouv.qc.ca/recherche/desclaureat.asp?noLaureat=391 Les Prix du Québec – la lauréate Victoria Kaspi]. (In French.)</ref>

==Early life and education==
Kaspi was born in [[Austin, Texas]], but her family moved to Canada when she was seven years old.<ref name="pmv"/> She completed her undergraduate studies at McGill in 1989, and went to [[Princeton University]] for her graduate studies, completing her [[PhD]] in 1993 supervised by [[Nobel Prize in Physics|Nobel Prize]]-winning astrophysicist [[Joseph Hooton Taylor, Jr.|Joseph Taylor]].<ref name="pmv"/><ref name="kqth"/>

==Career and research==
After a postdoc position at the [[California Institute of Technology]], the [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]], and a junior faculty position at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], she took a faculty position at McGill in 1999.<ref name="pmv"/> At McGill, she held one of McGill's first [[Canada Research Chair]]s,<ref name="bc">[https://www.mcgill.ca/reporter/33/09/additions/kaspi/ Victoria Kaspi], by Bronwyn Chester, ''McGill Reporter'', January 25, 2001.</ref> and in 2006 she was named the [[Lorne Trottier]] Professor of Astrophysics.<ref name="gazette">[http://www.canada.com/montrealgazette/news/story.html?id=0fdc401c-e705-4583-8429-40fe2ac1c573 Reaching for stars: juggling ambition, angst] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110604114559/http://www.canada.com/montrealgazette/news/story.html?id=0fdc401c-e705-4583-8429-40fe2ac1c573 |date=2011-06-04 }}, ''[[Montreal Gazette]]'', February 6, 2007.</ref> She is also a [[Fellow]] in the [[Canadian Institute for Advanced Research]]<ref name="cap" /> and the [[American Astronomical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Victoria Kaspi |url=https://www.mcgill.ca/researchhonours/victoria-kaspi |access-date=2025-06-11 |website=Research Honours |language=en}}</ref>

In 2015, Kaspi founded the McGill Space Institute and serves as its director.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://msi.mcgill.ca |title=McGill Space Institute |access-date=2025-02-21}}</ref> She has also served as director of the Gravity and the Extreme Universe program at the [[Canadian Institute for Advanced Research]] since 2017, and holds the title of Distinguished James McGill Professor.

Kaspi's observations of the pulsar associated with [[supernova remnant]] G11.2–0.3 in the constellation [[Sagittarius (constellation)|Sagittarius]], using the [[Chandra X-ray Observatory]], showed that the pulsar was at the precise center of the supernova, which had been [[History of supernova observation#Early history|observed in 386 CE]] by the Chinese. This pulsar was only the second known pulsar to be associated with a supernova remnant, the first being the one in the [[Crab Nebula]], and her studies greatly strengthened the conjectured relationship between pulsars and [[supernova]]e. Additionally, this observation cast into doubt previous methods of dating pulsars by their spin rate; these methods gave the pulsar an age that was 12 times too high to match the supernova.<ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/2001/01/11/us/scientists-find-second-pulsar-and-link-it-to-ancient-supernova.html Scientists Find Second Pulsar and Link It to Ancient Supernova], John Noble Wilford, ''[[New York Times]]'', January 11, 2001.</ref>

Kaspi's research with the [[Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer]] showed that [[soft gamma repeater]]s, astronomical sources of irregular [[gamma ray]] bursts, and [[anomalous X-ray pulsar]]s, slowly rotating pulsars with high [[magnetic field]]s, could both be explained as [[magnetar]]s.<ref name="cap"/><ref>[http://www.space.com/scienceastronomy/magnetars_020911.html Evidence Helps Confirm Existence of Powerful Magnetars], Robert Roy Britt, space.com, September 11, 2002.</ref>

She also helped discover the pulsar with the fastest known rotation rate, [[PSR J1748-2446ad]],<ref name="kqth"/> star clusters with a high concentration of pulsars,<ref name="kqth"/> and (using the [[Green Bank Telescope]]) the "cosmic recycling" of a slow-spinning pulsar into a much faster [[millisecond pulsar]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Scientists witness cosmic recycling first |date=May 22, 2009 |work=AdelaideNow |url=http://www.news.com.au/adelaidenow/story/0,22606,25520892-5012776,00.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110813125012/http://www.adelaidenow.com.au/news/breaking-news/scientists-witness-cosmic-recycling-first/story-e6frea73-1225714642221|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 13, 2011}}</ref><ref>[http://www.spacedaily.com/reports/Researchers_Catch_Nature_In_The_Act_Of_Recycling_A_Star_999.html Researchers catch nature in the act of "recycling" a star], Space Daily, May 22, 2009.</ref>

As part of her doctoral work with [[Joseph Hooton Taylor, Jr.|Joseph Taylor]], Kaspi conducted high-precision timing of [[millisecond pulsar]]s B1855+09 and B1937+21 using the [[Arecibo Observatory]]. This work produced the first upper limit on the energy density of a stochastic [[gravitational wave]] background using [[pulsar timing array]] techniques, constraining Ω<sub>g</sub>h<sup>2</sup> < 6 × 10<sup>−8</sup> at 95% confidence.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kaspi |first1=V. M. |last2=Taylor |first2=J. H. |last3=Ryba |first3=M. F. |title=High-Precision Timing of Millisecond Pulsars. III. Long-Term Monitoring of PSRs B1855+09 and B1937+21 |journal=[[The Astrophysical Journal]] |volume=428 |pages=713 |year=1994 |doi=10.1086/174280 |bibcode=1994ApJ...428..713K}}</ref> This result established the methodology later adopted by collaborations such as [[NANOGrav]], the [[European Pulsar Timing Array]], and the [[Parkes Pulsar Timing Array]].

In 2013, Kaspi's research group reported the first observation of an "anti-glitch"—a sudden spin-down event—in the [[magnetar]] 1E 2259+586, published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Archibald |first1=R. F. |last2=Kaspi |first2=V. M. |display-authors=etal |title=An anti-glitch in a magnetar |journal=Nature |volume=497 |issue=7451 |pages=591–593 |year=2013 |doi=10.1038/nature12159 |pmid=23719460 |bibcode=2013Natur.497..591A|arxiv=1305.6894 }}</ref> This was contrary to all previously observed pulsar glitches, which involve sudden spin-ups, and provided new constraints on the internal structure of neutron stars.

Kaspi is a lead scientist on the [[Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment]] (CHIME) [[Fast Radio Burst]] (FRB) project. Under her leadership, the CHIME/FRB collaboration detected hundreds of FRBs, dramatically expanding the known population and enabling statistical studies of their properties.<ref>{{cite journal |collaboration=CHIME/FRB |title=The First CHIME/FRB Fast Radio Burst Catalog |journal=[[The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series]] |volume=257 |issue=2 |pages=59 |year=2021 |doi=10.3847/1538-4365/ac33ab  |doi-access=free|arxiv=2106.04352 |bibcode=2021ApJS..257...59C}}</ref> This work contributed to her recognition as one of ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'''s 10 people who mattered in science in 2019.

==Personal life==
Kaspi is Jewish.<ref>{{cite news|first=Janice|last=Arnold|title=Jewish McGill Prof First Woman to Win Coveted Gerhard Herzberg Medal|date=6 June 2016|newspaper=Canadian Jewish News|url=http://www.cjnews.com/news/canada/mcgill-prof-uncomfortable-celebrity-status}}</ref> Her husband, David Langleben, is a [[cardiologist]] at McGill<ref name="bc"/> and at the [[Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital]] in Montreal.<ref name="gazette"/>
